Stock Investors Should Root for a Rate Hike. Yeah, Really.
 
Plus, winners and losers of the AI freakout
 

Assuming AI doesn’t end humanity, which would be pretty terrible for the stock market, the wave of caution is creating both winners and losers. Some hyperscalers spending all that money rose Monday, as did cybersecurity companies. But the broad effect on stock prices was negative, as was a rise in bond yields. That looks set to continue Tuesday.

9/15/2026, 6:38:20 AM ET
 
 
 

Pick your poison

 

Stock investors had better hope the Federal Reserve raises rates tomorrow. Yes, seriously—it beats the alternative.

 

For at least the past 15 years, the most important thing for them to know on almost any given day was what rate setters might be thinking. When some piece of economic news was clearly good, such as higher-than-expected jobs growth, it was basically a coin flip whether the S&P 500 would rise or fall. 

 

Good news could be bad news if it increased the odds of a hike, which was seen as a drag on stock prices—especially rate-sensitive tech companies.

 

Sometimes the economic tea leaves were hard to read, but loose-lipped Fed officials left little to chance. By the time decision day came around, it was a foregone conclusion.

 

The Fed’s late July meeting when it held rates steady, Kevin Warsh’s first as chair, wasn’t like that. Many bond traders were betting on a hike and were wrong.

 

Warsh’s clumsy explanation played a role in pushing up longer-term interest rates set by the bond market. On Monday, the 10-year Treasury note’s yield crossed 5%, hitting its highest intraday level since 2007.

 

That benchmark, not the overnight rate decided by human beings at the Fed, is what really matters to stock prices and to home buyers. Doubts about how committed Fed rate setters are to tackling inflation have hurt the central bank’s sway over the bond market. The market reaction to leaving rates unchanged again could be a repeat of July, or worse. 

 

“There’s something about Kevin Warsh that I don’t fully trust,” said Jeffrey Gundlach, probably the world’s most influential bond fund manager, on a podcast last week.

 

Gundlach, chief investment officer at DoubleLine Capital, said that he “would expect long-term interest rates to rise fairly significantly in the aftermath” of a decision to hold rates steady.

 

That would be a far bigger surprise than last time around, in no small part because of Warsh’s tough talk on inflation at a gathering of central bankers last month. The market-implied chance of a hike was one-third in mid-August and two-thirds after his speech, according to CME FedWatch. It’s now 95%.

 

Meanwhile, the gap between the 2-year Treasury note’s yield and the Fed’s overnight rate widened to a multiyear high Monday. That usually suggests the bond market expects a rate increase, and this time it pencils in at least one more quarter-point increase soon.

 

A vocal objection to a hike tomorrow might come from President Trump, who appointed Warsh and wants him to cut rates. But, like they say, “be careful what you wish for.”

 

One or two rate increases will hardly affect Main Street, or Wall Street for that matter. 

 

An out-of-control Treasury market sure would.
